problem.title: On-device visual inspection
problem.context: A manufacturer inspects parts for defects with cameras along 40 lines across three plants. Each line has two to four cameras and a fixed ARM edge computer with a small neural accelerator. Plant network links can be unavailable for days. Inspectors label about 5,000 images per week, and the model is retrained weekly and deployed to devices. The team is two ML engineers and a half-time operations engineer, with a tight infrastructure budget.

requirements.text: Check every part as it passes the camera and signal a defective part to the line operator.
Retrain the model every week from the newly labelled images and roll the new model out to every line.
Collect the images the model was unsure about, or got wrong, so that inspectors can label them.
Each image is classified on the line within 200 ms, so the line never slows down.
When a plant's network is down for up to seven days, its lines keep inspecting with the model they have; the images collected in the meantime are uploaded when the network returns.
A new model reaches every connected line within 24 hours of approval. When a new model misbehaves on a line, the line operator can go back to the previous one within 15 minutes, without the ML team.
Cloud and infrastructure spending stays under 2,000 euros a month.
Three people build and run the system, with no support outside working hours.
The edge computers (an ARM processor with a small neural accelerator) cannot be replaced this year.

points.description: The application contains the model as a module in a modular monolith and exposes predictions through a local service/API. Batch-ingested data feeds a scheduled model-building pipeline; CI/CD deploys validated models, supports rollback, and MLOps monitors logged inputs and predictions in production. Trade-off: This provides repeatable training, automated delivery, quality checks, observability, and a quick recovery path. It gives up immediate adaptation to new data because ingestion and retraining are batch- and schedule-based, and the modular-monolith structure may limit independent scaling of the model component.

The system ingests continuous data, periodically runs an automated training, evaluation, and validation pipeline, and uses CI/CD to deploy model services. Multiple model versions serve real-time predictions concurrently, with canary testing and performance monitoring guiding production decisions. Trade-off: This provides repeatable operations, controlled rollout, version comparison, and observable performance. It gives up immediate adaptation to streamed data because training is batch-based and schedule-triggered, while multiple services and monitoring increase operational complexity.

The model is embedded in a monolithic application and exposed for real-time predictions through a local service/API. Data is manually ingested, models are built in a development sandbox and batch-trained on a schedule, then deployed using scripts with rollback to a previous version when needed. Trade-off: This is simple and inexpensive to operate, with predictable scheduled updates and a recovery path. It gives up automated, reproducible delivery, continuous data or model oversight, and quality assurance because ingestion, deployment, monitoring, and testing are manual or absent.

The application embeds the model in its monolith and exposes predictions through a local service/API. Batched data feeds a scheduled, automated training and validation pipeline; CI/CD deploys models, supports rollback, and MLOps monitors data and predictions while performance tests verify the prediction service. Trade-off: This provides repeatable operations, controlled releases, rollback, and observable serving, but batch ingestion, offline learning, and scheduled runs reduce responsiveness to new data. Embedding the model simplifies local serving but couples model changes and deployment to the application.

1. Each model runs as its own local service/API, providing real-time predictions to the application. Batch-ingested data feeds a scheduled pipeline that trains, evaluates, validates, and delivers models through CI/CD, using canary testing before release; production performance is monitored and a prior version can be restored if needed. 2. Trade-off: This provides repeatable automation, controlled rollout, observability, and rapid rollback, but scheduled batch learning can leave models stale between runs and does not support immediate adaptation to new data. Separate services, monitoring, canarying, and rollback also increase operational complexity.

The application contains the model as a module in a modular monolith, serving predictions through a hybrid of online services and offline batch computations. Batch-ingested data feeds scheduled training, evaluation, validation, and model-quality testing; CI/CD deploys resulting versions, with monitoring of data and predictions and rollback support. Trade-off: This provides repeatable MLOps, operational visibility, and recoverability while supporting both timely and bulk scoring. It gives up continuous learning and potentially fresher models because ingestion and training are batch- and schedule-based, while the modular monolith limits independent scaling.

The application embeds the model in its monolith and exposes predictions through a local service/API, using batched data and scheduled pipeline runs for automated training, evaluation, and validation. CI/CD deploys models, canary testing and prediction-service performance tests protect releases, while monitoring logs data and predictions and rollback restores a previous version when needed. Trade-off: This provides repeatable operations, controlled releases, and recoverability without a separate model-serving deployment. Trade-off: Embedding couples model updates to the application, while batch ingestion and scheduled training reduce responsiveness to new data and limit rapid adaptation.

A separate model service exposes real-time predictions through a local API, while batch ingestion feeds a scheduled pipeline that trains, evaluates, and validates models offline. MLOps and CI/CD automate pipeline and deployment workflows; canary testing controls releases, monitoring logs data and predictions, and rollback restores the previous model version when needed. Trade-off: This provides repeatable operations, safer releases, observability, and recovery, but batch learning and scheduled runs reduce responsiveness to fresh data, while separate services and monitoring add operational complexity and deployment overhead.

The model is packaged as a module in a modular monolith, with batched data ingestion feeding scheduled, batch-based training and an automated build, evaluation, and validation pipeline. A hybrid serving layer provides online and offline predictions, while MLOps, CI/CD, canary testing, performance tests, monitoring, and logging support controlled deployment and rollback to earlier model versions. Trade-off: This gains repeatable automation, operational visibility, and safer releases, but batch ingestion and training reduce data freshness and responsiveness to new patterns. The modular-monolith integration also limits independent scaling compared with a separately deployed model service.

approaches.idea: What if inference and image collection stay local at each line, while a scheduled batch pipeline handles weekly training and rollout?
What if each model is an independently deployed service, with controlled multi-version or canary rollout?
What if the team minimizes platform work with manual ingestion, development-tool training, and scripts?
approaches.dropped_because: The approach relies on manual ingestion and release work and omits testing and production monitoring; it cannot reliably deliver the weekly rollout and image collection with this small team.

approaches.idea: What if hybrid online and offline serving complements a modular on-device application while keeping training and delivery automated?

trajectory.hypothesis: Local serving should keep R1 and Q1 independent of plant connectivity; scheduled batch training should support R2; logging may help R3 but does not explicitly select uncertain or wrong images.

tradeoffs.note: Scheduled batch retraining is practical for weekly labels but does not itself specify selective image capture or seven-day edge buffering and later upload.

trajectory.observation: The point combines local real-time serving with the automated weekly training and rollback path. Nothing attests this combination. The space does not establish inference timing, offline image buffering, or target infrastructure cost.

trajectory.hypothesis: Independent services, multiple versions, and canary testing should improve controlled rollout, but distributed real-time serving may fail R1 and Q2 during plant network outages.

tradeoffs.note: Separately managed services and concurrent versions support rollout control, but network-dependent inference threatens inspection continuity during outages.

trajectory.observation: The control-plane ideas are useful, but the service-based inference path conflicts with the outage requirement. A local serving choice could preserve the deployment approach while fixing that weakness. Nothing attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: A monolithic local service and scripts could lower service overhead, but manual ingestion, absent monitoring, and absent tests are likely to miss R2, R3, Q3, and C1's operating limits.

tradeoffs.note: Scripts and minimal platform features reduce service overhead, while manual delivery and no oversight or tests shift too much recurring work and release risk to the small team.

trajectory.observation: Local serving supports inspection, but the simplified operating model leaves image triage and upload unspecified and cannot provide dependable automated weekly delivery. Nothing attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Simplifying the edge integration to a monolith and adding prediction-service performance testing should make Q1 more directly verifiable while preserving local inspection, weekly retraining, and rollback.

tradeoffs.note: Batch collection and scheduled retraining support weekly updates but do not represent selective uncertainty capture or disconnected image queues.

trajectory.observation: The local API and explicit performance testing make the inference path clearer, though no threshold or benchmark is encoded in the space. Nothing attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Keeping a separate model service but serving it locally should address outages; canary testing plus rollback should improve Q3 while retaining independent deployment.

tradeoffs.note: A separate service and canary workflow can isolate releases, but they add operational components and cost without a budget figure or staffing model in the space.

trajectory.observation: Moving inference local resolves the major weakness of the seed while preserving independently deployable model services. Canaries and rollback still need a tested operator workflow to meet the 15-minute target. Nothing attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Hybrid online and offline serving may support immediate line inference alongside bulk work, while local modular integration and automated batch training retain outage tolerance and weekly retraining.

tradeoffs.note: Online service predictions and offline batches cover two serving modes, but the values do not specify image triage, buffering duration, or reconnect upload behavior.

trajectory.observation: The hybrid value offers a useful fit for online inspection plus bulk processing, but leaves the exact edge fallback and capture queue unspecified. Nothing attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Canary testing alongside performance tests should add release protection to the strongest local-first point without weakening weekly training or rollback.

tradeoffs.note: Batch-based updates support predictable weekly retraining but do not define selective capture or an offline upload buffer.

trajectory.observation: Canary testing improves release control, and performance testing targets the latency concern, but the design space offers no numeric pass threshold or measured rollback procedure. Nothing attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Combining the separately deployable local service with canary testing, performance monitoring, and an explicit rollback option should make the service-based approach safer to operate.

tradeoffs.note: Independent services and controlled rollout improve release flexibility but increase service management and infrastructure overhead.

trajectory.observation: The point retains the distinct service-per-model deployment boundary and avoids relying on the plant network for predictions. Canarying and rollback are appropriate controls, but their time limits and operating cost remain unproven. Nothing attests the combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Adding canary rollout and prediction performance testing should improve confidence in releases and Q1 while retaining the hybrid serving option.

tradeoffs.note: Hybrid online and batch serving with scheduled training supports inspection and weekly updates, but it does not specify selective capture or seven-day disconnected storage and upload.

trajectory.observation: Canarying and performance tests strengthen safeguards while preserving hybrid online and offline scoring. The search did not establish numeric latency, outage buffering, cost, or staffing results. Nothing attests the combination.

alternatives.name: Monolithic edge inference with controlled weekly releases
alternatives.summary: Run the model in the line application through a local API, and use scheduled batch training, automated deployment, canary checks, performance tests, monitoring, and rollback. This minimizes edge service boundaries while retaining a repeatable release process.

choices.reason: Embeds inference in the application on the existing edge installation, avoiding a remote inference dependency.
A local real-time API fits per-image line inspection and can keep serving when plant connectivity is lost.
Batched ingestion can move collected images and new labels into the recurring training flow.
choices.fit_note: The value says batch ingestion but does not specify uncertainty selection, local retention for seven days, or automatic upload after reconnection.

adrs.title: How should line inference and image collection work?
adrs.context: Every part needs a timely prediction, including during long network outages. Capturing images for later labeling also requires local persistence and reconnect upload behavior, but the design space names serving and batch ingestion without a value for edge buffering or uncertainty-based selection.

options.name: Monolithic local API
pros: Keeps the model deployment boundary simple.
cons: Batch ingestion does not specify offline buffering or selective image capture.
options.reason: Chosen for a direct local inference path and small edge footprint; implement the missing image queue explicitly.

options.name: Independent local service
pros: Local inference remains available without plant connectivity.
Model deployment can be separated from the host application.
cons: Adds another service to deploy and operate.
The data collection mechanism remains unspecified.
options.reason: Chosen where independent model releases justify a separate local service.

options.name: Hybrid online and offline serving
pros: Covers online prediction and offline batch processing.
cons: Does not define that online predictions stay local through outages or how images are buffered.
options.reason: Chosen when batch scoring complements line inference and the team can define the edge fallback explicitly.

options.name: Network-dependent microservice
pros: Separates serving and supports continuous data ingestion.
cons: A network-dependent inference path risks stopping inspection during a plant outage.
options.reason: Set aside because it misses the availability need of the line.

adrs.title: How should weekly learning and production feedback be handled?
adrs.context: New labels arrive every week, while uncertain or incorrect images must be collected and retained across outages. Scheduled batch learning fits the cadence, but the space has no explicit value for active-learning selection or a durable local image queue.

options.name: Scheduled batch training with logged predictions
pros: Automates repeatable weekly training and validation.
Logging gives a starting point for inspector review.
cons: Logging does not itself select uncertain images or guarantee delayed upload after an outage.
options.reason: Chosen to meet the known weekly cadence and provide useful production records, with the capture queue specified as a required implementation gap.

options.name: Manual ingestion and development-tool training
cons: Manual handling does not provide dependable weekly retraining or image collection at this scale.
options.reason: Set aside because recurring manual work is unreliable for the small team.

adrs.title: How should model rollout and recovery be controlled?
adrs.context: Approved models must reach connected lines promptly, and an operator must be able to restore a previous version quickly. Automation and staged rollout reduce manual exposure but add operating components for a small team.

options.name: Automated local rollout with canary and rollback
pros: Automates delivery and supports staged exposure and recovery.
Reduces reliance on the ML engineers for routine releases.
cons: The space does not demonstrate 24-hour delivery, a 15-minute operator rollback, or operational fit for three people.
options.reason: Chosen for all three alternatives because deployment automation, canary testing, and rollback directly support the release workflow.

options.name: Build and deployment scripts
pros: Can be inexpensive and simple for a small prototype.
cons: Manual script operation and absent MLOps increase recurring work and release risk.
options.reason: Set aside because the process does not provide enough automation or oversight for 40 lines.

options.name: Prediction performance testing
cons: The space does not set a 200 ms threshold or provide benchmark results.
options.reason: Chosen for the monolithic and hybrid alternatives to make latency testing explicit.

options.name: Canary testing in the model test dimension
pros: Provides a staged check before broad rollout.
cons: Does not establish how quickly an operator can roll back.
options.reason: Chosen for the independently deployed service alternative as a rollout safeguard.

unaddressed.note: The space has no infrastructure-cost or budget dimension, so it cannot establish whether any alternative stays below 2,000 euros per month.
The space has no dimension for ARM/neural-accelerator compatibility, model format, or hardware replacement constraints; local serving alone does not prove compatibility.
